column2: The Cape Campaign: Imperial Garrisons Defeated

The commandos have secured the British-held Cape districts, from the western ports to the eastern frontier. The raad demands a complete imperial withdrawal, the incorporation of Zululand and Mabhudu, and protection over Swaziland and Basutoland. The occupation gives our delegates a strong position at the conference, but victory in the field must become an agreement binding both governments. Customs officers, merchants and district councils await the settlement that will determine their future. The commandants urge the government to secure the gains for which their men have fought, while the treasury presses for demobilisation and a return to ordinary trade.
Carry these demands to the peace conference.
The Cape Conference: A Republic from Sea to Frontier

The treaty has been signed. The commandos have secured the British-held Cape and compelled the imperial government to withdraw. The western ports and Cape districts pass under republican sovereignty, while Zululand and Mabhudu are incorporated and Swaziland and Basutoland enter the republic's protection. The extraordinary mobilisation ends, but the work of peace begins. Customs offices, councils, farms and roads must function under their new administration. A delegation will open discussions with Bloemfontein within the month, preparing articles of union for the two Boer republics. The raad intends to bring those articles before a conference after six months of consolidation. London confronts a crisis, while Pretoria must show that victory can sustain a government as well as an army.
Ratify the treaty. Let the republic endure beyond the victory!
The Cape Lost: An Imperial and Constitutional Crisis

News of the Cape capitulation reaches a country shaken by the scale of defeat. Ministers face inquiries over the war, merchants question the loss of ports and trade, and republican committees accuse the Crown of binding itself to a disastrous imperial policy. Parliament establishes a republic amid demonstrations and bitter disputes over responsibility. The new administration inherits debt, distrust and an empire whose subjects now see weakness at its centre. Reconstruction will require more than a change of flag. Irish nationalists prepare to test the government, while the treasury and armed services demand reform. Ministers must restore public confidence, preserve commerce and decide how much of the old imperial system their exhausted country can still support.
Establish a republic and convene a reconstruction parliament.
Ireland and the Broken Imperial Settlement

The defeat overseas has transformed the argument at home. Irish nationalists insist that a British republic cannot claim government by consent while denying the same principle across the Irish Sea. Committees and volunteers move to proclaim an Irish administration in the districts still held by Britain. London can recognise that government and negotiate peace, or contest the separation by force. The new republic's ministers must decide whether their promised constitutional renewal extends beyond Britain itself.
Recognise Irish independence and negotiate a settlement.
Contest the rising and restore British authority by force.
The Orange Articles Are Ready for Conference

Six months of correspondence, accounts and district consultations have brought the proposed union to the conference table. Pretoria and Bloemfontein have exchanged drafts on customs, public debts, representation and the authority of the local raads. The Orange delegates still have to ratify the agreement, but both governments can now consider a common republic on terms their districts have had time to examine. Our delegation will carry the final invitation south. Unity will ask the victorious government to reconcile different traditions of administration, rather than merely extend its orders across a frontier. The conference must give those traditions a durable place in the institutions of South Africa.
Invite the Orange delegation to the conference.
A Common Republic: The Orange Delegation

Transvaal proposes a union after its extraordinary victory at the Cape. The invitation offers the Orange districts a place in a common South African republic rather than continued separation between neighbouring Boer administrations. A common customs system and foreign policy promise greater strength, but the Orange delegates ask how their raad, public accounts and district institutions will be represented. Acceptance transfers the Free State's administration and territory to the northern republic before a new South African constitution is proclaimed. Refusal preserves independence and requires renewed negotiation, rather than an automatic annexation or war.
Join the conference and accept a common republic.
Preserve the independence of the Orange Free State.
The Orange Articles of Union

The delegates have agreed to unite the two republican administrations. District records, public obligations and territory pass into the common government, while the proclamation will establish its national institutions. The Orange raad's representatives have secured a place in the founding assembly, and commissioners must reconcile the accounts and customs systems of the two republics. Farmers and merchants look for easier passage across the old frontier. The commandants seek a common defence, while district councils ask how their authority will be respected. The articles settle the question of union, but their value will be measured by the government's ability to turn these promises into ordinary public administration.
Ratify the articles and summon the founding raad.
The Republic of South Africa Proclaimed

From Pretoria and Bloemfontein to the Cape ports, the delegates proclaim one Republic of South Africa. The victory that secured its territory could not by itself create a nation: the articles of union now join the administrations and ask their people to build institutions capable of surviving peace. The Transvaal government becomes the common South African state, uniting public accounts, armed forces and district institutions. Boer traditions remain central to the founding settlement, but the republic governs communities with different languages and histories. Its constituent districts must decide the balance between local councils and the presidency, and whether citizenship will remain narrow or become a broader civic compact. The founding constitution opens a choice of government paths, followed by decisions for schools, defence and Cape administration.
Proclaim the republic and convene its constituent assembly.
The Founding Constitution

The constituent raad must choose how the new republic will be governed. Delegates have come from districts with different laws, debts and traditions of public authority. A district federation would give local councils a strong place in the settlement, preserving familiar institutions while creating a common government for foreign affairs and defence. A central presidency would concentrate administration and military command in national institutions, promising firmer coordination across the enlarged territory. Advocates of a civic compact urge the raad to broaden political participation and invest in schools, public service and the reception of newcomers. These proposals raise questions that victory alone cannot answer: who speaks for the republic, how its revenue is spent, and what obligations bind its districts together. The articles chosen here will guide the work of the ministries and shape the relationship between the capital and the people it governs.
A federation of district raads.
A strong national presidency.
A broader civic compact.

The complete Cape peace provides five years of stronger administration.

Demand Complete Cape Capitulation
